content:
There are, in my opinion, two very different types of gacha game developers.

The first type is represented by large companies such as miHoYo and Hypergryph. They have professional data teams, experienced community managers, and enough manpower to continuously produce new content. This allows them to maintain a large player base, keep the game fresh, and constantly monitor and adjust the game’s balance.

The second type consists of smaller companies and indie studios. They lack manpower and experience, but they have one major advantage: they can actually become part of their own community. They can listen to players more closely and create content specifically tailored to what their players want. Their player base may be much smaller than that of a major developer, but the community is often more cohesive, engaged, and loyal.

What makes Morimens so strange to me is that it seems to have the disadvantages of a small studio without fully taking advantage of the advantages that a small studio should have.

I completely understand that the team is small. I understand that there may not be enough manpower, that employees may leave, and this can lead to a lack of content and slower development. I think most players are willing to accept a transition period because of that.

What I find difficult to accept is that the developers repeatedly contradict their own previous statements and make promises that eventually feel meaningless. In other words, they are gradually consuming the trust that players have placed in them.

content:
When Final Law +12 was introduced, the developers explicitly stated that it was not intended to pressure players into spending more money, that the team had not become greedy, and that future content would not be designed around +12.

But what do we have now?

D-Tide has been continuously getting harder. And this isn’t just about the latest update. In previous versions as well, each new D-Tide was more difficult than the one before it.The affection system was also changed.

And the frustrating part is that none of these changes seem to be responding to what the community has actually been asking for. In fact, I believe it would not be difficult for the developers to predict that these changes would receive negative feedback from the community before implementing them. Yet they were implemented anyway.

The feedback regarding the Poison and Counter mechanics is another example. The response was essentially, “We tested it, and there were no problems.”

But tested under what conditions?

What was the testing methodology? What data did you collect? What benchmarks were used?

There was very little explanation of the actual basis for that conclusion. From the perspective of player experience and the numerical design of the new version, the development team’s so-called testing results simply aren’t convincing enough.

This is especially disappointing because gacha games have many different ways of monetizing their player base.

You don’t have to keep increasing the difficulty in order to encourage players to spend money.

There are skins. UI packages. Background music packs. Cosmetic items. Merchandise. And many other forms of monetization that can generate revenue without damaging the fundamental gameplay experience.There are plenty of ways to make money without constantly pushing the difficulty curve upward.
thread_title: Pls listen to the community (long post warning)

content:
I also understand that D-Tide is supposed to be the endgame content that the developers consider important. I understand why you continue to increase its difficulty and experiment with different mechanics.

But at the same time, other game modes such as Train and D-Dive have received far less attention and refinement.

The difficulty gap between different Train bosses can be enormous, and the numerical inflation in some encounters is honestly absurd.

Please spend some of your development resources creating new game modes and improving existing ones.Please don’t keep focusing almost exclusively on D-Tide.Giving players some gacha currency and upgrade resources every two weeks isn’t going to destroy your revenue.

Morimens has an excellent foundation. That’s precisely why I care enough to write all of this.

However, since the game came close to shutting down and subsequently came back, I’ve also noticed a number of warning signs.

Sometimes, the producer gives me the impression of an “arrogant, strong-minded indie game developer” who has a very specific vision and is unwilling to compromise—someone who decides what they want to do and simply goes ahead with it.

There is nothing inherently wrong with having your own vision as a game designer.

But there is a difference between having a vision and refusing to listen.

What I would really like to see is a development team that is willing to put down its pride, listen to the community, and seriously consider what players are telling you.

Being a small studio should not mean that you have to imitate the weaknesses of large developers. In fact, your size could be your greatest advantage if you were able to communicate with and respond to your community more directly.

Unfortunately, what we are seeing right now is a situation where the game is both developed by a small team and, at the same time, repeatedly making decisions that feel like a betrayal of the players’ trust.
thread_title: Pls listen to the community (long post warning)

content:
I don’t know whether the development team will actually accept this criticism.

But I genuinely believe that Morimens is a good game.That’s why I am worried.

After everything the game has been through, especially after coming so close to shutting down and then being brought back, I don’t want to see it slowly walk toward the same danger again.

I sincerely hope that the developers can recognize these warning signs, rebuild the trust of the community, and make better use of the strengths that a small development team can have.

I want Morimens to become better and better, and to be around for many, many years.

I was sold on the premise of the 'dead game that resurrected itself' reputation Morimens had: hard but fair content, a small developer team that cares, a community that reciprocates this passion in turn. Decided to monetarily support the game heavily by normal standards. The recent changes introduced in v2.6 put to question this view I have of BIAV and Morimens as a whole.

New Awakener introduces a terrain-exclusive talent that is ripe for exploitation mechanics- and FOMO-wise. Endgame mode is exponentially harder and inaccessible to the vast majority of players for a paltry return in resources. Mobs, Elites, and Bosses introduced on Chapter 6 invalidates entire categories of teams; in the same update that gave us an HP scaler, a Boss can remove total HP at thrice the efficacy AND starts at 75% health. Just the one boss invalidates Poison, Counter, Sustain teams and April's Tribute users in one go.
